scenes.tts: How can fertilizer spread far upstream leave the Bay's bottom short of oxygen? The fertilizer never grabs oxygen itself. Follow this cross-section from a field to the Bay's deep channel. The missing oxygen comes from a living chain, helped by summer water.

scenes.visual: Keep the same moving cross-section dimly visible. Show the title Where the Bay's Oxygen Goes for two seconds, then return the landscape to full contrast.

scenes.tts: A watershed is all the land that drains into one river, lake, or bay. Rain becomes runoff when it flows over the ground. Orange nutrient markers join that water from fields, lawns, wastewater, and the air. Here, nutrients mean nitrogen and phosphorus.
scenes.caption: A watershed is all the land that drains into one river, lake, or bay. Rain becomes runoff when it flows over the ground. Orange nutrient markers join that water from fields, lawns, wastewater, and the air. Here, nutrients mean nitrogen and phosphorus.
scenes.visual: Outline the full watershed in orange around the carried landscape. Animate rain, then a widening stream that carries orange markers from four simple labelled sources. Keep the field, river, Bay, and bottom oxygen gauge in their established positions.
scenes.narration: A watershed is all the land that drains into one river, lake, or bay. Rain becomes runoff when it flows over the ground. Orange nutrient markers join that water from fields, lawns, wastewater, and the air. Here, nutrients mean nitrogen and phosphorus.

scenes.tts: The orange markers reach sunlit surface water. Green algae multiply, turning a thin layer into a thick bloom. The bloom shades the gold grass below. Some algae also grow on grass blades. Less light reaches the leaves, while dead algae begin sinking.
scenes.caption: The orange markers reach sunlit surface water. Green algae multiply, turning a thin layer into a thick bloom. The bloom shades the gold grass below. Some algae also grow on grass blades. Less light reaches the leaves, while dead algae begin sinking.
scenes.visual: Transform arriving orange markers into a spreading green surface bloom labelled algal bloom. Sunbeams shorten as the bloom thickens. Gold grass dims. Turn some green algae pale and animate them sinking toward the deep channel.
scenes.narration: The orange markers reach sunlit surface water. Green algae multiply, turning a thin layer into a thick bloom. The bloom shades the gold grass below. Some algae also grow on grass blades. Less light reaches the leaves, while dead algae begin sinking.

scenes.tts: At the bottom, bacteria break down the dead algae. Bacteria are decomposers, living things that break down dead matter. They use blue dissolved oxygen while they work. Dissolved oxygen is oxygen gas mixed into water. Fish, crabs, and oysters need it.
scenes.caption: At the bottom, bacteria break down the dead algae. Bacteria are decomposers, living things that break down dead matter. They use blue dissolved oxygen while they work. Dissolved oxygen is oxygen gas mixed into water. Fish, crabs, and oysters need it.

scenes.visual: Hold the question and both gauges for thinking. Keep only slow water drift and tiny bacterial motion. Do not reveal either gauge changing.

scenes.tts: The bottom gauge falls first. Fresh river water floats above saltier, heavier seawater in summer. The boundary slows mixing. Surface water still exchanges oxygen with the air. Below, decomposition keeps using oxygen, but replacement is slow. Water this low in oxygen is hypoxia.
scenes.caption: The bottom gauge falls first. Fresh river water floats above saltier, heavier seawater in summer. The boundary slows mixing. Surface water still exchanges oxygen with the air. Below, decomposition keeps using oxygen, but replacement is slow. Water this low in oxygen is hypoxia.
scenes.visual: Lower only the bottom gauge as blue dots continue disappearing. Show a broad oxygen arrow entering the surface from air, then bending along the layer boundary instead of reaching deep water. Label the low bottom region hypoxia while the fish swims upward.
scenes.narration: The bottom gauge falls first. Fresh river water floats above saltier, heavier seawater in summer. The boundary slows mixing. Surface water still exchanges oxygen with the air. Below, decomposition keeps using oxygen, but replacement is slow. Water this low in oxygen is hypoxia.

scenes.tts: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and bacteria decompose faster when it is warm. That strengthens the summer shortage. So the deep channel runs shortest on oxygen in summer, not winter.
scenes.caption: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and bacteria decompose faster when it is warm. That strengthens the summer shortage. So the deep channel runs shortest on oxygen in summer, not winter.
scenes.visual: Run a schematic season strip above the same cross-section from spring runoff to summer warmth. A warm-water icon speeds bacterial pulsing. The bottom blue gauge dips further while the layer boundary stays closed. Mark every curve and gauge schematic.
scenes.narration: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and bacteria decompose faster when it is warm. That strengthens the summer shortage. So the deep channel runs shortest on oxygen in summer, not winter.

scenes.tts: The chain also has a delay. Much nitrogen arrives with high river flow in late winter and spring. Algae grow, die, and sink over time. Decomposition can continue into summer, so scientists use spring nutrient inputs when forecasting summer hypoxia.

scenes.visual: Keep the same landscape under a wide schematic calendar. Move orange markers inland-to-Bay during late winter and spring, then transform them into green bloom and sinking pale algae. Extend bacterial motion into summer while the bottom blue gauge falls later.
scenes.narration: The chain also has a delay. Much nitrogen arrives with high river flow in late winter and spring. Algae grow, die, and sink over time. Decomposition can continue into summer, so scientists use spring nutrient inputs when forecasting summer hypoxia.

scenes.tts: This process is eutrophication: nutrient enrichment feeds too much algae and can lead to oxygen loss. Animals that can leave low oxygen move away. Others may sicken or die. Follow the cause carefully. Nutrients start the chain, while living things use the oxygen.

scenes.visual: Compress the carried landscape into one continuous arrow path across the frame: orange nutrients, green bloom, pale sinking algae, bacteria, falling blue gauge. Keep the layer boundary behind the path. Never draw fertilizer touching oxygen.

scenes.tts: Low oxygen is not the only effect. The surface bloom and algae on grass blades block sunlight. That can weaken underwater grass habitat, a second harm that does not depend on low oxygen. Weather changes the outcome, but human nutrient inputs remain a pressure people can reduce.
